analysis.one_liner: Directed the President to negotiate a free trade area with Mexico and the Caribbean.
analysis.headline: The bill to launch North American free trade negotiations died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the President to negotiate a free trade agreement with Mexico and the Caribbean Basin countries, aiming at a North American free trade area. It also let the President sign trade deals with any developing country, giving that country up to five years to phase out its trade barriers while the US opened faster. Once a deal was signed, it would take effect automatically unless Congress passed a law rejecting it within 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: US exporters and multinational companies would gain tariff-free access to Mexican and Caribbean markets, and consumers would pay less for imported goods. The bill's own findings argue that mutual tariff cuts raise incomes in every country involved and that free trade spurs development abroad [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Exporters, multinationals, and consumers buying imports

how_it_helps.text: It ordered the President to open negotiations with Mexico and the Caribbean Basin countries to eliminate tariffs and other trade barriers, creating a larger duty-free market for US exporters [S3].

It authorized the President to sign trade agreements with any developing country, letting that country phase out its barriers gradually over up to five years while the US side opened faster — an asymmetric deal aimed at pulling developing economies into open trade [S3].
It gave the President authority to exclude specific sensitive products from a deal when needed to reach agreement, a flexibility that makes deals easier to close [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and communities in industries that compete with imports — apparel, electronics assembly, light manufacturing — would face new competition as tariff walls came down. The bill contains no adjustment assistance, retraining, or compensation for displaced workers. The Treasury would also forgo tariff revenue, since cutting duties is the bill's core mechanism [S3].

drawbacks.text: It shifted trade power to the executive branch: once the President signed an agreement, it would enter into force automatically unless both chambers passed a disapproval bill within 90 days — a high bar under expedited procedures — and the President could then cut tariffs by proclamation without a separate vote [S3].

Opening the US market to lower-wage neighbors would expose import-competing manufacturers and their workers to sudden competition, and the bill offered them nothing in return — no retraining, no transition aid, no safeguard process beyond the President's own termination power [S3].

A fair-minded supporter would concede the gains are diffuse and the losses concentrated: cheaper goods and bigger export markets benefit everyone a little, while job losses fall hard on specific towns and industries, and the bill's five-year phase-in for developing countries gives US workers little protection during the transition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursued real gains — larger export markets, cheaper imports, and, by its reasoning, pressure toward open trade abroad — but its design gave the President sweeping authority with only a passive congressional check, and it did nothing for the workers whose jobs the opening would put at risk. With zero cosponsors, the bill was a one-man initiative whose trade-offs were never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the entire two-year Congress and died when that Congress ended, without a hearing, a cosponsor, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Phil Gramm introduced the bill on February 7, 1989, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, trade policy stayed exactly where it stood in early 1989. Import-competing manufacturers and their workers avoided the faster market opening the bill would have set in motion, though the broader push for a North American trade agreement moved ahead later through other channels.

for.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the President to negotiate a North American free trade area; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or vote; it sat in committee for the full Congress until it expired.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. The sponsor was a Texas Republican, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee simply never acted, so no partisan split on the merits can be measured.

industries.note: The bill's central purpose was to win them duty-free access to Mexico and the Caribbean. Their gain came partly at the expense of import-competing US workers, though consumers shared some benefit through lower prices.

industries.industry: Import-competing manufacturers (apparel, electronics assembly, light manufacturing)
industries.note: Tariff elimination with lower-wage neighbors would have exposed these industries to direct competition. Their fate and the fate of their production workers rise and fall together.
Cheaper imported goods mean lower costs for retailers and lower prices for shoppers, so this industry's gain runs alongside consumers'.
Cutting tariffs is the bill's core mechanism, so federal tariff revenue would shrink; that cost is spread across all taxpayers rather than falling on any one group.
